content: 1. In 1752, there was a one-day discrepancy between the date in England and the date in other European countries. 2. In England, the date continued to be recorded as usual until September 2, 1752. The following day was recorded as September 14, 1752, skipping 11 days. 3. Dates recorded under the older Julian calendar system can be represented using double dating. 4. For example, a date originally recorded as March 24, 1750, would correspond to March 24, 1751, in the modern Gregorian calendar. Using double dating, it would be written as March 24, 1750/51. 5. A concrete example illustrates the potential for confusion: In 1715, France used the Gregorian calendar, with the year starting on January 1. England, however, used the Julian calendar, with the year starting on March 25. In England, the year 1700 was a leap year, but in France, it was not. As a result, June 10, 1715, in England appeared to be 11 days earlier than June 21, 1715, in France. England continued the same year until late March, so February 15, 1715, in England corresponded to February 26, 1716, in France. In Scotland, which still used the Julian calendar, the same day was February 15, 1716. 6. For events occurring before 1752 in countries still using the Julian calendar, it is best to use double dating whenever the exact year can be determined. 7. When transcribing an original record where the exact year is evident but not explicitly stated, the double date can be written, for example, as March 24, 1750. 8. It is important to note that in places using the old Julian calendar, the numbering of months also varied. 9. In the Julian calendar, March was considered the 1st month of the year, April the second, May the third, and so on. 10. The 24 days in March that fell before the beginning of the year were generally regarded as part of the first month. 11. Note: The above information may apply to British genealogical records but does not necessarily apply to records in other countries. 12. A notable exception is the Nordic countries, particularly Sweden, which have detailed and mostly accurate church records from the 18th century onward. 13. However, as with any historical research, a critical review of all information and an assessment of the reliability of each source is required. Reliability of Sources 14. Information found in historical or genealogical sources can be unreliable, and it is good practice to evaluate all sources critically. 15. Factors influencing the reliability of genealogical information include: The knowledge of the informant (or writer). The bias and mental state of the informant (or writer). The passage of time and the potential for copying and compiling errors. Knowledge of the Informant 16. The informant is the individual who provided the recorded information. 17. Genealogists must carefully consider who provided the information and what they knew. 18. In many cases, the informant is identified in the record itself. 19. For example, a death certificate usually has two informants: a physician who provides information about the time and cause of death, and a family member who provides details such as the birth date and names of parents. 20. When the informant is not identified, one can sometimes deduce their identity by carefully examining the source. 21. One should first consider who was alive (and nearby) when the record was created. 22. When the informant is also the person recording the information, handwriting can be compared to other samples. 23. If a source does not provide clues about the informant, genealogists should treat the source with caution. 24. Such sources can still be useful if they can be compared with independent sources. 25. For example, a single census record cannot be given much weight because the informant is unknown. 26. However, when multiple censuses over several years agree on a piece of information unlikely to be guessed by a neighbor, it is likely that the information was provided by a family member or another informed person. 27. On the other hand, information in a single census cannot be confirmed by an undocumented compiled genealogy, as the genealogy may have used the census record as its source and could therefore depend on the same misinformed individual. Bias and Mental State of the Informant 28. Even individuals with knowledge of the facts sometimes intentionally or unintentionally provided false or misleading information. 29. A person may have lied to obtain a government benefit (such as a military pension), avoid taxation, or cover up an embarrassing situation (such as the existence of a non-marital child). 30. A person in a distressed state of mind may not be able to accurately recall information. 31. Many genealogical records were created at the time of a loved one’s death, so genealogists should consider the effect that grief may have had on the informant of these records. The Effect of Time 32. The passage of time often affects a person’s ability to recall information. 33. As a general rule, data recorded soon after an event is usually more reliable than data recorded many years later. 34. However, different types of data are more difficult to recall after many years than others. 35. Dates, in particular, are especially prone to recollection errors. 36. The ability to recall is also affected by the significance of the event to the individual. 37. These values may have been influenced by cultural or individual preferences. Copying and Compiling Errors 38. Genealogists must consider the effects that copying and compiling errors may have had on the information in a source. 39. Sources are generally categorized into two types: original and derivative. 40. A derivative source is information taken from another source. 41. An original source is one that is not based on another source. 42. Each time a source is copied, information may be lost, and errors may arise from the copyist misreading, mistyping, or miswriting the information. 43. Genealogists should consider the number of times information has been copied and the types of derivation a piece of information has undergone. 44. Types of derivatives include photocopies, transcriptions, abstracts, translations, extractions, and compilations. 45. In addition to copying errors, compiled sources (such as published genealogies and online pedigree databases) are susceptible to misidentification errors and incorrect conclusions based on circumstantial evidence. 46. Identity errors usually occur when two or more individuals are assumed to be the same person. 47. Circumstantial or indirect evidence does not explicitly answer a genealogical question but may be used with other sources to answer the question, suggest a probable answer, or eliminate certain possibilities. 48. Compiled sources sometimes draw hasty conclusions from circumstantial evidence without sufficiently examining all available sources, without properly understanding the evidence, and without appropriately indicating the level of uncertainty. The Maximum Relationship 49. One area of interest in biology, shared by some genealogists, is determining the maximum degree of separation that currently exists among all people in the world. 50. This refers to how many generations back the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the two most distantly related people on Earth lived. 51. Recent models, accounting for factors such as sexual differentiation, monogamy, and realistic migration patterns, suggest that the MRCA of all humans likely lived 75–150 generations, or 2,000–4,000 years, ago. 52. Furthermore, these models suggest that the MRCA likely lived somewhere in Southeast Asia, increasing the likelihood of their descendants reaching the remote islands of the Pacific.
